hypothesis: Weather foundation models such as Aurora and GraphCast, which autoregressively generate high-resolution multi-variable forecasts at orders of magnitude lower computational cost than NWP systems, could be directly fine-tuned as upstream forecast engines for renewable energy planning pipelines, replacing the bespoke numerical weather prediction inputs currently used by solar and wind power forecasters. Because these models already predict surface wind components, 2-metre temperature, and solar-relevant variables at 6-hour resolution globally, their probabilistic trajectory outputs could be ingested by grid scheduling optimizers to dramatically reduce the worst-case day-ahead forecast errors—which have grown from ~3 GW to over 13 GW in Europe—while simultaneously cutting the computational overhead of the combined weather-to-dispatch pipeline. This tight coupling of Earth-system foundation models with renewable dispatch optimization could enable real-time, uncertainty-aware unit commitment at scales previously infeasible with either NWP or standalone ML forecasters.

Simultaneously, the renewable energy planning literature identifies that solar/wind forecast errors are growing rapidly and that grid scheduling—an NP-hard problem—urgently needs faster, higher-quality weather inputs to manage variable generation (solnet-pv:1, tackling-climate-ml:4, tackling-climate-ml:6, tackling-climate-ml:63).
